parsed.explanation: The combined regime is split. At the national layer the traveller meets the sharpest exposure: passport sex-marker rules, an 'X' marker no longer processed, a February 2025 cable directing officers to refuse cases with document discrepancies and to weigh lifetime ineligibility for material misrepresentation, and documented abuse in immigration custody. Those follow every visitor at the border. Inside the division, however, the operative picture is genuinely protective: public-accommodation law covering gender identity with an enforcement body, no facility ban, open marker-change rules, functioning hate-crime enhancement, and a most-protective risk tier. The division's protections do not reach the national border desk or national custody, so the score sits in the Elevated band — materially better than a criminalising jurisdiction, materially below a jurisdiction whose working protections also cover entry and custody.

entry_documents.exposure: National executive order bars self-selected markers and foreign-ministry processing of X markers; February 2025 cable directs officers to refuse cases with document discrepancies and consider lifetime ineligibility for material misrepresentation.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; misrepresentation finding is never automatic and requires four elements; litigation ongoing and some orders enjoined.
entry_documents.interaction: Division's open state documents do not reach national passport or visa issuance; the traveller clears national, not division, document rules at the border.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody documents forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse of transgender men; national corrections policies impose conversion-style practices.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: A legal-aid organisation maintains a FAQ on passport and identity-document rules; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A document discrepancy at entry can flow into national detention, where the division's anti-discrimination law has no purchase.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars transgender people from federally funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; 9 states ban facility use in all government buildings, 4 criminalise certain bathroom use in public buildings.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has no facility ban; its public-accommodations law covers facilities, and its risk tier is the most-protective tier.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: A visitor staying within the division avoids the facility bans, but transiting or crossing into a neighbouring jurisdiction enters a materially different environment.

care_services.exposure: National orders target gender-affirming care for minors; travel insurance and emergency care questions for outed travellers are unresolved.
care_services.protection: April 2023 state executive order directs agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming care within the division, including for people travelling in; hospital records must protect gender-identity data.
care_services.interaction: The division's shield reaches in-division providers but the dossier does not describe its effect on out-of-division subpoenas or on national facilities.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups as a priority; national rhetoric frames gender ideology as extremist, and a rewards memorandum uses that phrase.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division bars discrimination, bars the panic defence, and the chief legal office sued school boards whose policies out trans students.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National threat framing does not control the division's police, but it colours the national border and investigative layer the traveller passes through.

minors_guardians.exposure: National executive order directs law enforcement to investigate schools facilitating a minor's social transition and to prosecute teachers; national care bans for minors apply in 27 states.
minors_guardians.protection: This division has no such ban; its guidance promotes name/pronoun policies, and its chief legal office litigated against parental-notification policies.
minors_guardians.interaction: A parent travelling with a trans minor child would face national border and custody exposure but a protective division environment for schools and services.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National hate-crime reporting for gender identity is uneven across states; the criminalisation of bathroom use in some states creates arrest risk for the visibly trans.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division has bias-crime enhancements, sensitivity training, a police-licensing system of gender-identity protections, and ranks among the safest per-capita measured rates; the panic defence is barred.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Violence data show legal hostility does not predict where trans women are killed; the division's own combination of low violence and working protections is the operative picture inside its borders.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Lifetime ineligibility and refusal-of-entry decisions are discretionary and appeal-dependent; the passport suits and executive-order challenges are unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: A division civil-rights enforcement body investigates and can grant relief; legal aid maintains guidance on the national rules.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: The traveller's remedy for an adverse border decision lies in the national system, not the division's, so the strong local remedies do not reach the exposure

anchor_checks.comparison: Both involve denial at the border with an administrative regime and no detention. This case is worse: the national cable also contemplates a lifetime ineligibility finding and the dossier documents abusive immigration custody, both above the anchor's mere exclusion and confiscation, so it rates above.

Comparable: an adverse administrative flag is worked through a written guideline with a supervisor's intervention, giving a temporary permit and no detention. Here the adverse flag is national and discretionary rather than appealable on the spot, but the division offers real service and accommodation recourse, so the rating is similar.

In that anchor the privacy directive worked in the encounter and the director apologised, and the only risk was a downstream legacy database. Here the operative authority at the border is the restrictive national rule, not the division's protective law, so this case sits materially lower.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller experiences two regimes stacked. The national layer owns the border, document screening, visa framing and immigration custody, and there it holds the whole exposure: a visitor flagged on mismatched or unavailable markers may be questioned, refused or found permanently ineligible, and any detention that follows falls under a custody record documented as abusive. The division layer owns daily life, and there it is close to the best available: public accommodation, lodging, care, facilities, hate-crime remedies and low measured violence. Neither layer is role of law-free, but a division's local enforcement cannot follow the traveller to the national desk, and the local exposure does not match the national burden, so that the score sits above the hostile facially unrestricted options and below the low-risk options.
